# Choosing the Link for Binary Y

::: {style="display:none"}
$\newcommand{\VS}{\quad \mathrm{VS} \quad}$
$\newcommand{\and}{\quad \mathrm{and} \quad}$
$\newcommand{\E}{\mathbb E}$
$\newcommand{\P}{\mathbb P}$
$\newcommand{\Var}{\mathbb V}$
$\newcommand{\Cov}{\mathrm{Cov}}$
$\newcommand{\1}{\mathbf 1}$
:::

. . .

> ⬅ **Previous:** [Introduction to the Generalized Linear Model](Introduction_glm.qmd)  ·  **Next:** [Models for Categorical Data](categorical_data.qmd) ➡

## Outline of the Chapter

- **Binary response**: choosing the link function (logit, probit, cloglog)
- **Interpretation**: odds and odds ratios
- **Estimation**: maximum likelihood; uniqueness, existence, asymptotic normality
- **Inference**: Wald tests, confidence intervals, deviance tests, AIC/BIC
- **Prediction**: confidence interval for $p(x)$, classification, ROC curve

## Context

. . .

$Y$ is a binary variable [$Y_k \in \{0,1\}$]{style="background-color: lightblue;"}

. . .

$X = (X^{(1)}, \ldots, X^{(p)})$ are $p$ regressors

. . .

$Y|X = x$ follows a [Bernoulli distribution]{style="background-color: yellow;"} with parameter [$p(x) = P(Y = 1|X = x)$]{style="background-color: lightblue;"}. We model it as

. . .


::: {.square-def}
$$p(x) = g^{-1}(x^T\beta)$$
:::


where $g^{-1}$ is a [strictly increasing function]{style="background-color: yellow;"} with values in $[0, 1]$

. . .

**First question**: how to choose $g^{-1}$ (equivalently, the link function $g$)?



## Example: Coronary Heart Disease


. . .

**Data**: presence of coronary heart disease (chd) as a function of age, with $Y = \text{chd} \in \{0,1\}$ and $X = \text{age}$

. . .

**Goal**: estimate [$p(x) = \E(Y|X = x) = \P(\text{chd} = 1|X = x)$]{style="background-color: lightblue;"} for every $x$

::: {style="font-size:80%"}
100 patients; duplicated ages are stacked. **Hover** for values, **toggle** layers below.
:::

```{=html}
  var N=AGE.length;
  function erf(z){var s=z<0?-1:1;z=Math.abs(z);var t=1/(1+0.3275911*z);return s*(1-((((1.061405429*t-1.453152027)*t+1.421413741)*t-0.284496736)*t+0.254829592)*t*Math.exp(-z*z));}
  function Phi(x){return .5*(1+erf(x/Math.SQRT2));}
  function sig(t){return 1/(1+Math.exp(-t));}
  var L={
    logit:{col:'#e74c3c',F:sig,f:function(t){var p=sig(t);return p*(1-p);}},
    probit:{col:'#3498db',F:Phi,f:function(t){return Math.exp(-t*t/2)/2.5066282746;}},
    cloglog:{col:'#27ae60',F:function(t){return 1-Math.exp(-Math.exp(t));},f:function(t){return Math.exp(t-Math.exp(t));}}
  };
  // MLE by Fisher scoring (IRLS), age centred at 45 for stability
  function fit(l){
    var a=0,b=0,XC=45;
    for(var it=0;it<100;it++){
      var S0=0,S1=0,S2=0,T0=0,T1=0;
      for(var i=0;i<N;i++){
        var x=AGE[i]-XC,e=a+b*x,m=Math.min(1-1e-10,Math.max(1e-10,l.F(e))),d=Math.max(l.f(e),1e-12);
        var w=d*d/(m*(1-m)),z=e+(CHD[i]-m)/d;
        S0+=w;S1+=w*x;S2+=w*x*x;T0+=w*z;T1+=w*x*z;
      }
      var D=S0*S2-S1*S1,na=(S2*T0-S1*T1)/D,nb=(S0*T1-S1*T0)/D,dd=Math.abs(na-a)+Math.abs(nb-b);
      a=na;b=nb;if(dd<1e-12)break;
    }
    l.b0=a-b*XC;l.b1=b;

  var CL=[[20,30],[30,35],[35,40],[40,45],[45,50],[50,55],[55,60],[60,70]];

    function X(a){return ml+(a-x0)/(x1-x0)*(W-ml-mr);}
    function Y(p){return H-mb-(p-y0)/(y1-y0)*(H-mt-mb);}
    function IX(px){return x0+(px-ml)/(W-ml-mr)*(x1-x0);}
    function pos(e){var r=cv.getBoundingClientRect();return [(e.clientX-r.left)*W/r.width,(e.clientY-r.top)*H/r.height];}
    var KEY='glmChd_'+id,on={};

    try{var sv=JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem(KEY));if(sv)on=sv;}catch(e){}
    function save(){try{localStorage.setItem(KEY,JSON.stringify(on));}catch(e){}}
    var hover=null;
    [['cls','age classes'],['logit','logit'],['probit','probit'],['cloglog','cloglog']].forEach(function(bb){
      var b=document.createElement('button');b.className='lm-btn'+(on[bb[0]]?' on':'');b.textContent=bb[1];
      b.onclick=function(){on[bb[0]]=!on[bb[0]];b.classList.toggle('on',!!on[bb[0]]);save();draw();};
      row.appendChild(b);

    function hatB(sub,x,y){ // β̂₀ drawn with a real caret
      var yb=y+5;c.textBaseline='alphabetic';c.fillText('β'+sub,x,yb);var w=c.measureText('β').width,cx=x+w/2;
      c.beginPath();c.moveTo(cx-3.5,yb-13);c.lineTo(cx,yb-17);c.lineTo(cx+3.5,yb-13);c.stroke();c.textBaseline='middle';

      c.clearRect(0,0,W,H);c.fillStyle='#fff';c.fillRect(0,0,W,H);

      c.textAlign='center';c.textBaseline='top';

        });

    cv.addEventListener('pointermove',function(e){var p=pos(e),a=IX(p[0]);hover=(p[0]>=ml&&p[0]<=W-mr&&a>=19.5&&a<=69.5)?Math.round(a):null;draw();});
    cv.addEventListener('pointerleave',function(){hover=null;draw();});
    draw();

})();
```

## Example: GLM Approach



. . .

**Objective**: model $p(x) = P(\text{chd} = 1|X = x)$ as
$$p(x) = g^{-1}(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x)$$

. . .

**Constraint**: $g^{-1}$ must take values in $[0, 1]$, since $p(x)$ is a probability

## Example: The Logit Model



. . .

:::{style="font-size: 60%;"}
::: {.square-def}

$$g^{-1}(t) = \frac{e^t}{1 + e^t} \quad \text{i.e.} \quad g(t) = \ln\left(\frac{t}{1-t}\right) = \text{logit}(t)$$

:::
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size:80%"}
Curve: $g^{-1}(\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1 x)$ with $\hat\beta$ obtained by MLE. **Hover** to read $\hat p(x)$.
:::

## Which Link Function for Binary Y?



. . .

**Question**: which link function should we choose in practice when $Y$ is binary?

. . .

**Default choice**: we favor the [**logit model**]{style="background-color: yellow;"}

. . .

**Exceptions**: unless there is a good reason to choose another link (probit, complementary log-log, or log-log)

. . .

**Next steps**: we revisit the 3 usual choices to justify this preference

## Details on the Probit Model



. . .

The probit model is justified when the binary variable $Y|X = x$ comes from thresholding a Gaussian latent variable $Z(x)$:

::: {.square-def}
$$(Y|X = x) = \mathbf{1}_{Z(x) \geq \tau}$$
:::
where [$Z(x) \sim \mathcal{N}(x^T\beta, \sigma^2)$]{style="background-color: lightblue;"}

. . .

With $\Phi$ the CDF of $\mathcal N(0,1)$, we get
$$P(Y = 1|X = x) = P(Z(x) \geq \tau) = \Phi\left(\frac{x^T\beta - \tau}{\sigma}\right)$$


## Examples in Probit Model




- $Y$ is a purchase decision, and $Z(x)$ quantifies the [utility]{style="background-color: yellow;"} of the good
- $Y$ is a declared psychological state (happiness, depression) and $Z(x)$ is an [unobserved (latent) measure]{style="background-color: yellow;"} of personal satisfaction

## Probit vs Logit: Current Trends



. . .

**Econometricians**: the [probit model]{style="background-color: yellow;"} remains fairly popular among [econometricians]{style="background-color: yellow;"}...

. . .

**General trend**: ...but it tends to be [replaced by the logistic model]{style="background-color: yellow;"}

. . .

**Advantages of logit**: the [logit model has many advantages]{style="background-color: yellow;"} that probit lacks:

- Interpretation of results
- Explicit formulas

. . .

**Theoretical justification**: the probit CDF is close to the logit CDF


## Remarks on cloglog Model



. . .

The model is $p(x) = g^{-1}(x^T\beta)$ with

::: {.square-def}
$$g(t) = \ln(-\ln(1-t)) \quad \text{i.e.} \quad g^{-1}(t) = 1 - e^{-e^t}$$
:::



. . .

It is not symmetric, in the sense that [$g(t) \neq -g(1-t)$]{style="background-color: lightblue;"}.

$p(x)$ approaches $0$ slowly but $1$ very rapidly.

. . .

If the opposite holds (fast to $0$, slow to $1$), take $g(t) = -\ln(-\ln(t))$ (loglog model).

. . .

cloglog is useful in [survival models]{style="background-color: yellow;"} (e.g. the Cox model).


## Details on the Logit Model



1. A highly valued interpretation tool: odds ratios.

2. More convenient from a theoretical point of view.

3. A natural model in many situations.


## Theoretical Motivation of Logit



. . .

We will show in the exercises that:

[If]{style="background-color: orange;"}, in the two groups $Y = 0$ and $Y = 1$, $X$ is Gaussian with different means $m_0 \neq m_1$ (and the same covariance $\Sigma$),

::: {.square-def}
$X|(Y = 0) \sim \mathcal N(m_0, \Sigma) \and X|(Y = 1) \sim \mathcal N(m_1, \Sigma)$
:::



[then]{style="background-color: orange;"} $\mathbb P(Y = 1|X = x)$ follows a logistic model.

. . .

The result still holds for two distributions of the same exponential family (with sufficient statistic $x$) that differ only by their natural parameter.


## Summary for Binary Variables



. . .

If $Y$ is a binary variable, [$(Y|X = x) \sim \mathcal B(p(x))$]{style="background-color: lightblue;"}.

In a GLM for $Y$, we set $p(x) = g^{-1}(x^T\beta)$ where $g$ is:

- [by default the logit]{style="background-color: yellow;"} function, which is the most natural;



- [possibly probit]{style="background-color: yellow;"} if we have good reasons to justify it (but the results will be similar to logit);


- [cloglog (or loglog)]{style="background-color: yellow;"} if we have good reasons to justify it ([strong asymmetry of $p(x)$]{style="background-color: yellow;"}, connection with a Cox model).

. . .


From now on, we [focus on the logit model]{style="background-color: yellow;"}.

## The Logit Model in One Picture {.smaller}

::: {style="font-size:90%"}
$Y|X=x$ is a **Bernoulli** variable around the mean curve $p(x)=\text{logit}^{-1}(\beta_0+\beta_1x)$. **Move** $\beta_0,\beta_1$, then compare with the other GLMs.
:::

```{=html}
<script>
(function () {
  var cv=document.getElementById('gxC'); if(!cv||cv.dataset.init)return; cv.dataset.init=1;
  var c=cv.getContext('2d'),W=cv.width,H=cv.height,KEY='glmExplorerLogit',eq=document.getElementById('gxEq');
  var s0=document.getElementById('gxB0'),s1=document.getElementById('gxB1'),v0=document.getElementById('gxB0v'),v1=document.getElementById('gxB1v');
  var mBtns=[].slice.call(cv.parentNode.querySelectorAll('button[data-m]'));
  var CFG={
    G:{b0:[-3,5,1],b1:[-1,1.5,.8],y:[-4,14],tk:[0,4,8,12],tex:'Y\\mid X=x\\sim\\mathcal N(\\mu(x),\\sigma^2),\\quad \\mu(x)=\\beta_0+\\beta_1x'},
    B:{b0:[-8,4,-4],b1:[-2,2,.8],y:[-.12,1.12],tk:[0,.5,1],tex:'Y\\mid X=x\\sim\\mathcal B(\\mu(x)),\\quad \\mathrm{logit}\\,\\mu(x)=\\beta_0+\\beta_1x'},
    P:{b0:[-2,2.5,-.3],b1:[-.4,.4,.28],y:[-1,20],tk:[0,5,10,15,20],tex:'Y\\mid X=x\\sim\\mathcal P(\\mu(x)),\\quad \\ln\\mu(x)=\\beta_0+\\beta_1x'}
  };
  var mode='G',n=90,ux=[],uu=[],gz=[],uj=[],SIG=1.5,XS=[1,3,5,7,9];
  for(var i=0;i<n;i++){ux[i]=Math.random()*10;uu[i]=Math.random();var a=0,b=0;while(!a)a=Math.random();while(!b)b=Math.random();gz[i]=Math.sqrt(-2*Math.log(a))*Math.cos(2*Math.PI*b);uj[i]=Math.random()-.5;}
  function sig(t){return 1/(1+Math.exp(-t));}
  function mu(x){var e=+s0.value+(+s1.value)*x;return mode==='G'?e:mode==='B'?sig(e):Math.exp(Math.min(e,6));}
  function qpois(u,m){var k=0,p=Math.exp(-m),s=p;while(u>s&&k<300){k++;p*=m/k;s+=p;}return k;}
  function typesetEq(){if(window.MathJax&&MathJax.Hub&&MathJax.Hub.Queue)MathJax.Hub.Queue(['Typeset',MathJax.Hub,eq]);else setTimeout(typesetEq,200);}
  function setMode(m,keep){
    mode=m;var q=CFG[m];
    s0.min=q.b0[0];s0.max=q.b0[1];s1.min=q.b1[0];s1.max=q.b1[1];
    if(!keep){s0.value=q.b0[2];s1.value=q.b1[2];}
    mBtns.forEach(function(b){b.classList.toggle('on',b.dataset.m===m);});
    eq.innerHTML='\\('+q.tex+'\\)';typesetEq();
  }
  function draw(){
    var q=CFG[mode],lo=q.y[0],hi=q.y[1],ml=46,mr=16,mt=10,mb=34;
    v0.textContent=(+s0.value).toFixed(2);v1.textContent=(+s1.value).toFixed(2);
    function X(x){return ml+(x+.2)/10.8*(W-ml-mr);} function Y(v){return H-mb-(v-lo)/(hi-lo)*(H-mt-mb);}
    c.clearRect(0,0,W,H);c.fillStyle='#fff';c.fillRect(0,0,W,H);c.lineWidth=1;c.font='13px sans-serif';
    c.fillStyle='#666';c.textAlign='right';c.textBaseline='middle';
    q.tk.forEach(function(v){c.strokeStyle=v===0?'#ccc':'#eee';c.beginPath();c.moveTo(ml,Y(v));c.lineTo(W-mr,Y(v));c.stroke();c.fillText(v,ml-7,Y(v));});
    c.textAlign='center';c.textBaseline='top';for(var x=0;x<=10;x+=2)c.fillText(x,X(x),H-mb+5);
    c.fillStyle='#333';c.fillText('x',(ml+W-mr)/2,H-mb+18);
    c.save();c.beginPath();c.rect(ml,mt,W-ml-mr,H-mt-mb);c.clip();
    // sample, drawn from fixed uniforms so it morphs smoothly
    for(var i=0;i<n;i++){var m=mu(ux[i]),y=mode==='G'?m+SIG*gz[i]:mode==='B'?(uu[i]<m?1:0)+uj[i]*.06:qpois(uu[i],m);
      c.beginPath();c.arc(X(ux[i]),Y(y),3.2,0,7);c.fillStyle='rgba(44,62,80,.45)';c.fill();}
    // conditional distributions of Y | X = x, drawn sideways
    var WD=58;
    XS.forEach(function(x0){
      var m=mu(x0),bx=X(x0);
      c.strokeStyle='rgba(0,0,0,.25)';c.beginPath();c.moveTo(bx,mt);c.lineTo(bx,H-mb);c.stroke();
      c.fillStyle='rgba(52,152,219,.22)';c.strokeStyle='#3498db';
      if(mode==='G'){
        c.beginPath();c.moveTo(bx,Y(m-3.5*SIG));
        for(var t=-3.5;t<=3.5;t+=.1)c.lineTo(bx+WD*Math.exp(-t*t/2),Y(m+t*SIG));
        c.lineTo(bx,Y(m+3.5*SIG));c.closePath();c.fill();c.stroke();
      }else if(mode==='B'){
        [[0,1-m],[1,m]].forEach(function(r){c.fillRect(bx,Y(r[0])-6,WD*r[1],12);c.strokeRect(bx,Y(r[0])-6,WD*r[1],12);});
        c.fillStyle='#2471a3';c.textAlign='left';c.textBaseline='bottom';c.fillText(m.toFixed(2),bx+4,Y(1)-8);
      }else{
        var pk=0,p=Math.exp(-m),pm=[];for(var k=0;k<=hi;k++){pm.push(p);pk=Math.max(pk,p);p*=m/(k+1);}
        var th=Math.max(3,Math.min(9,(Y(0)-Y(1))*.7));
        pm.forEach(function(pp,k){c.fillRect(bx,Y(k)-th/2,WD*pp/pk,th);});
      }
      c.beginPath();c.arc(bx,Y(m),5,0,7);c.fillStyle='#e74c3c';c.fill();
    });
    // mean curve
    c.strokeStyle='#e74c3c';c.lineWidth=3;c.beginPath();
    for(var j=0;j<=300;j++){var xx=-.2+10.8*j/300;j?c.lineTo(X(xx),Y(mu(xx))):c.moveTo(X(xx),Y(mu(xx)));}c.stroke();
    c.restore();c.lineWidth=1;
    c.font='14px sans-serif';c.textAlign='left';c.textBaseline='middle';
    c.strokeStyle='#e74c3c';c.lineWidth=3;c.beginPath();c.moveTo(ml+12,mt+14);c.lineTo(ml+36,mt+14);c.stroke();c.lineWidth=1;
    c.fillStyle='#333';c.fillText('E(Y | X = x) = g⁻¹(β₀ + β₁x)',ml+44,mt+14);
    c.fillStyle='rgba(52,152,219,.5)';c.fillRect(ml+12,mt+30,24,10);c.fillStyle='#333';c.fillText('law of Y | X = x',ml+44,mt+35);
    try{localStorage.setItem(KEY,JSON.stringify({m:mode,b0:+s0.value,b1:+s1.value}));}catch(e){}
  }
  mBtns.forEach(function(b){b.onclick=function(){setMode(b.dataset.m);draw();};});
  s0.addEventListener('input',draw);s1.addEventListener('input',draw);
  var sv=null;try{sv=JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem(KEY));}catch(e){}
  if(sv&&CFG[sv.m]){setMode(sv.m,true);s0.value=sv.b0;s1.value=sv.b1;}else setMode('B');
  draw();
})();
</script>
```

## Roadmap for the Logit Model

- **Interpretation**: what does a coefficient $\beta_j$ mean?
- **Estimation**: compute $\hat\beta$ by maximum likelihood; when does it exist?
- **Inference**: tests and confidence intervals on $\beta$, model comparison
- **Prediction**: estimate $p(x)$ for a new individual, classify it

# Model Interpretation

## Outline: Interpretation

- How the sign and size of $\beta_j$ shape $p(x)$
- A running example: the BMI study
- Odds and odds ratios
- In logistic regression, the odds ratio is $e^{\beta_j}$


## Interpretation of the Logistic Model

. . .

For $x=(x^{(1)}, \dots, x^{(p)}) \in \mathbb R^{p \times 1}$,

::: {.square-def}
$$p(x) = \text{logit}^{-1}(x^T\beta) = \frac{e^{x^T\beta}}{1 + e^{x^T\beta}}$$
:::



- The map $x^{(j)} \to p(x)$ (other regressors fixed) is increasing if $\beta_j > 0$, decreasing if $\beta_j < 0$ (constant if $\beta_j = 0$).

- The larger $|\beta_j|$, the stronger the [discriminatory power]{style="background-color: yellow;"} of regressor $X^{(j)}$: a small change in $x^{(j)}$ can cause a large change in $p(x)$.

## Shape of the logistic curve {.smaller}



. . .


::: {style="font-size:90%"}
As a function of $x^{(j)}$ (other regressors fixed): the **sign** of $\beta_j$ gives the direction, $|\beta_j|$ the steepness, slope $\beta_j/4$ at $p=1/2$.
:::

```{=html}
(function () {

  var ml=60,mr=16,mt=14,mb=40,x0=-3,x1=3,y0=-.04,y1=1.04,KEY='glmShape';

  function Y(p){return H-mb-(p-y0)/(y1-y0)*(H-mt-mb);}

  function draw(){

    btns.forEach(function(b){b.classList.toggle('on',+b.dataset.b===b1&&b0===0);});
    c.clearRect(0,0,W,H);c.fillStyle='#fff';c.fillRect(0,0,W,H);c.font='14px sans-serif';c.lineWidth=1;
    c.fillStyle='#666';c.textAlign='right';c.textBaseline='middle';

    c.textAlign='center';c.textBaseline='top';

    c.save();c.beginPath();c.rect(ml,mt,W-ml-mr,H-mt-mb);c.clip();
    // midpoint p = 1/2 and tangent of slope βj/4
```

## Example: BMI Study (French: IMC)

. . .

For each of the 5301 patients, we observe:

- [$Y$: 1 if BMI > 35]{style="background-color: yellow;"}, 0 otherwise
- AGE
- DBP: diastolic blood pressure
- SEXE: male or female
- ACTIV: 1 if intense sports activity, 0 otherwise
- WALK: 1 if walking or cycling to work, 0 otherwise
- MARITAL: marital status (6 categories: married, widowed, divorced, separated, single or cohabiting)


## Model Definition



. . .

We model $P(Y = 1|X)$, where $X$ gathers all the previous variables except $Y$.

. . .

In R, we use the `glm` function with the option `family=binomial`:

```r
glm(Y ~ AGE + DBP + SEXE + ACTIV + WALK + MARITAL, family=binomial)
```


## Model Results



. . .

:::{style="font-size: 50%;"}
| Variable    | Estimate  | Std. Error | z value | Pr(>|z|)    | Significance |
|-------------|-----------|------------|---------|-------------|--------------|
| (Intercept) | -2.810240 | 0.294316   | -9.548  | < 2e-16     | ***          |
| AGE         | -0.004407 | 0.002717   | -1.622  | 0.105       |              |
| DBP         | 0.017581  | 0.003283   | 5.356   | 8.53e-08    | ***          |
| SEXEFEMME   | 0.544916  | 0.081261   | 6.706   | 2.00e-11    | ***          |
| WALK1       | -0.409344 | 0.095972   | -4.265  | 2.00e-05    | ***          |
| ACTIV1      | -0.789734 | 0.126653   | -6.235  | 4.51e-10    | ***          |
| MARITAL2    | 0.070132  | 0.149638   | 0.469   | 0.639       |              |
| MARITAL3    | -0.071318 | 0.127510   | -0.559  | 0.576       |              |
| MARITAL4    | 0.188228  | 0.206598   | 0.911   | 0.362       |              |
| MARITAL5    | 0.070613  | 0.115928   | 0.609   | 0.542       |              |
| MARITAL6    | -0.150165 | 0.157687   | -0.952  | 0.341       |              |
:::

. . .

The table reads as for a linear regression (estimates, standard errors, tests).

. . .

None of the MARITAL coefficients is significant: we want to remove MARITAL from the model.

## Model Results with AGE²



. . .
```r
glm(Y ~ AGE + I(AGE^2) + DBP + SEXE + WALK + ACTIV, family=binomial)
```

which gives:

. . .

:::{style="font-size: 50%;"}
| Variable    | Estimate   | Std. Error | z value | Pr(>|z|)    | Significance |
|-------------|------------|------------|---------|-------------|--------------|
| (Intercept) | -3.9564361 | 0.3155529  | -12.538 | < 2e-16     | ***          |
| AGE         | 0.0640837  | 0.0123960  | 5.170   | 2.34e-07    | ***          |
| I(AGE^2)    | -0.0006758 | 0.0001260  | -5.364  | 8.14e-08    | ***          |
| DBP         | 0.0121546  | 0.0033775  | 3.599   | 0.00032     | ***          |
| SEXEFEMME   | 0.5155651  | 0.0776229  | 6.642   | 3.10e-11    | ***          |
| WALK1       | -0.4042257 | 0.0913195  | -4.426  | 9.58e-06    | ***          |
| ACTIV1      | -0.6573558 | 0.1150226  | -5.715  | 1.10e-08    | ***          |
:::

For an individual with WALK1=0 and [ACTIV1=0]{style="background-color: yellow;"}:

:::{style="font-size: 50%;"}
$P(Y = 1|\text{AGE}, \text{DBP}) = \text{logit}^{-1}(-3.96 + 0.064 \times \text{AGE} - 0.00068 \times \text{AGE}^2 + 0.0122 \times \text{DBP})$
:::
. . .

For an individual with WALK1=0 and [ACTIV1=1]{style="background-color: yellow;"}:

:::{style="font-size: 50%;"}
$P(Y = 1|\text{AGE}, \text{DBP}) = \text{logit}^{-1}(-3.96 + 0.064 \times \text{AGE} - 0.00068 \times \text{AGE}^2 + 0.0122 \times \text{DBP} \color{red}{ - 0.657})$
:::


## Odds 




::: {.square-def}
$$\text{odds} = \frac{p}{1-p}$$

:::


. . .

**Betting interpretation**: odds of $3$ to $1$ mean that for every $3$ people betting on $A$, $1$ person bets on $B$.

. . .

So a randomly chosen bettor bets on $A$ with probability [$p=3/4$]{style="background-color: lightblue;"} and on $B$ with probability $1-p=1/4$.


## Odds given X=x



. . .

Similarly, the odds of $Y = 1$ given $X = x$ are

::: {.square-def}
$$\text{odds}(x) = \frac{p(x)}{1 - p(x)}$$
:::


. . .

where $p(x) = P(Y = 1|X = x)$.


## Odds Ratio



. . .

For two individuals with characteristics $x_1$ and $x_2$, the [odds ratio]{style="background-color: yellow;"} between $x_1$ and $x_2$ is

$$OR(x_1, x_2) = \frac{\text{odds}(x_1)}{\text{odds}(x_2)} = \frac{\frac{p(x_1)}{1-p(x_1)}}{\frac{p(x_2)}{1-p(x_2)}}$$

. . .

::: {.callout-warning}
[**DO NOT CONFUSE ODDS RATIO WITH PROBABILITY RATIO**]{style="background-color: orange;"}

Only possible exception: if $p(x_1)$ and $p(x_2)$ are both very small, then $1 - p(x_1) \approx 1$ and $1 - p(x_2) \approx 1$, so that $OR(x_1, x_2) \approx p(x_1)/p(x_2)$
:::


## Link with the Probability Ratio



. . .

However, the OR and the probability ratio are [always on the same side of $1$]{style="background-color: yellow;"}:

$$\begin{aligned}
OR(x_1, x_2) > 1 &\Leftrightarrow \frac{p(x_1)}{p(x_2)} > 1\\
OR(x_1, x_2) < 1 &\Leftrightarrow \frac{p(x_1)}{p(x_2)} < 1\\
OR(x_1, x_2) = 1 &\Leftrightarrow \frac{p(x_1)}{p(x_2)} = 1
\end{aligned}$$


## Another Property of the Odds Ratio

. . .

$OR(x_1, x_2)$ [accentuates the differences]{style="background-color: yellow;"}: it is further from $1$ than $p(x_1)/p(x_2)$:

$$\begin{aligned}
OR(x_1, x_2) > \frac{p(x_1)}{p(x_2)} &\text{ when } OR(x_1, x_2) > 1\\
OR(x_1, x_2) < \frac{p(x_1)}{p(x_2)} &\text{ when } OR(x_1, x_2) < 1
\end{aligned}$$


## Examples Using Odds Ratios

. . .

Logistic regression is most often used to compare the [behavior of two individuals]{style="background-color: lightgreen;"} with respect to [the variable of interest]{style="background-color: lightblue;"}.

. . .

Examples:

- [probability of purchase]{style="background-color: lightgreen;"} depending on whether or not one has been the [subject of a personalized promotion]{style="background-color: lightblue;"};
- [probability of a breakdown]{style="background-color: lightgreen;"} of a vehicle [according to its age]{style="background-color: lightblue;"};
- [probability of recovery]{style="background-color: lightgreen;"} according to the [treatment used]{style="background-color: lightblue;"}.


## Odds Ratio in Logistic Regression

. . .

In the logistic model, [$\text{odds}(x) = \frac{p(x)}{1 - p(x)} = \exp(x^T \beta)$]{style="background-color: lightblue;"}


Hence

::: {.square-def}
$OR(x_1, x_2) = \frac{\text{odds}(x_1)}{\text{odds}(x_2)} = \exp((x_1 - x_2)^T \beta)$
:::


. . .

If the two individuals differ only in regressor $j$:

$OR(x_1, x_2) = \exp(\beta_j (x_1^{(j)} - x_2^{(j)}))$

. . .

If regressor $j$ is binary ($x_1^{(j)} = 1$ and $x_2^{(j)} = 0$):

[$OR(x_1, x_2) = \exp(\beta_j)$]{style="background-color: lightblue;"}


## Key Summary Statement

. . .

In a logistic regression model, $\beta_j$ is the logarithm of the odds ratio between two individuals whose regressor $j$ differs by $1$, all else being equal.

. . .

**In brief:** [$\exp(\beta_j) = OR(x^{(j)} + 1, x^{(j)})$]{style="background-color: yellow;"}


If regressor $j$ is binary (presence or absence of a characteristic):

. . .

$\exp(\beta_j)$ is simply the OR between [presence and absence]{style="background-color: yellow;"} of this characteristic, all else being equal.


## Example 1: Intense Sports Activity

. . .

:::{style="font-size: 50%;"}
| Variable    | Estimate   | Std. Error | z value | Pr(>|z|)    | Significance |
|-------------|------------|------------|---------|-------------|--------------|
| (Intercept) | -3.9564361 | 0.3155529  | -12.538 | < 2e-16     | ***          |
| AGE         | 0.0640837  | 0.0123960  | 5.170   | 2.34e-07    | ***          |
| I(AGE^2)    | -0.0006758 | 0.0001260  | -5.364  | 8.14e-08    | ***          |
| DBP         | 0.0121546  | 0.0033775  | 3.599   | 0.00032     | ***          |
| SEXEFEMME   | 0.5155651  | 0.0776229  | 6.642   | 3.10e-11    | ***          |
| WALK1       | -0.4042257 | 0.0913195  | -4.426  | 9.58e-06    | ***          |
| ACTIV1      | -0.6573558 | 0.1150226  | -5.715  | 1.10e-08    | ***          |
:::

. . .

All else being equal, the OR between practicing and not practicing intense sports activity is

. . .

$\exp(-0.657) \approx 0.52$

. . .

The odds of obesity are therefore [roughly halved]{style="background-color: lightblue;"} for individuals who practice intense sports activity.


[**(The odds, not the probability!)**]{style="background-color: orange;"}


## Example 2: Diastolic Pressure

. . .

:::{style="font-size: 50%;"}
| Variable    | Estimate   | Std. Error | z value | Pr(>|z|)    | Significance |
|-------------|------------|------------|---------|-------------|--------------|
| (Intercept) | -3.9564361 | 0.3155529  | -12.538 | < 2e-16     | ***          |
| AGE         | 0.0640837  | 0.0123960  | 5.170   | 2.34e-07    | ***          |
| I(AGE^2)    | -0.0006758 | 0.0001260  | -5.364  | 8.14e-08    | ***          |
| DBP         | 0.0121546  | 0.0033775  | 3.599   | 0.00032     | ***          |
| SEXEFEMME   | 0.5155651  | 0.0776229  | 6.642   | 3.10e-11    | ***          |

:::

All else being equal, the OR for an increase of $+20$ in diastolic pressure is

. . .

$\exp(0.0121546 \times 20) \approx 1.28$

. . .

The odds of obesity therefore increase by [$28\%$]{style="background-color: lightblue;"}.


# Estimation of the Parameters

## Outline: Estimation

- Likelihood and log-likelihood of the logistic model
- The MLE has no closed form: numerical optimization
- Uniqueness (when $\text{rank}(X) = p$) and existence (when the classes overlap)
- Asymptotic normality of $\hat\beta$ and Fisher information

## The Framework

. . .

We observe $n$ i.i.d. realizations $(Y_i, X_i)$ where $Y_i \in \{0, 1\}$ and $X_i \in \mathbb{R}^p$.

. . .

We write $p(x_i) = P(Y_i = 1|X_i = x_i)$.

## The Logistic Model

. . .

We assume the logistic model: for all $i$,

::: {.square-def}
$$p(x_i) = \text{logit}^{-1}(x_i^T \beta) = \frac{e^{x_i^T \beta}}{1 + e^{x_i^T \beta}}$$
:::



. . .

where $\beta = (\beta_1, \ldots, \beta_p)^T$ and $x_i^T \beta = \beta_1 x_i^{(1)} + \cdots + \beta_p x_i^{(p)}$.

## Parameter Estimation

. . .

::: {.square-def}
$$p(x_i) = \text{logit}^{-1}(x_i^T \beta) = \frac{e^{x_i^T \beta}}{1 + e^{x_i^T \beta}}$$
:::

We will estimate $\beta$ by [maximizing the likelihood]{style="background-color: yellow;"}.

. . .

We write [$p_\beta(x_i)$]{style="background-color: lightblue;"} instead of $p(x_i)$ to emphasize its dependence on $\beta$.


## Likelihood Calculation

. . .

For each $i$, $Y_i|(X_i = x_i)$ follows the Bernoulli distribution $B(p_\beta(x_i))$, so

:::{style="font-size: 80%;"}
::: {.square-def}
$$P(Y_i = y_i|X_i = x_i) = p_\beta(x_i)^{y_i}(1 - p_\beta(x_i))^{1-y_i}$$
:::

:::


. . .

for all $y_i \in \{0, 1\}$.

## Likelihood

. . .

By independence, we obtain the likelihood

::: {.square-def}
$$\ell(\beta, y_1, \ldots, y_n, x_1, \ldots, x_n) = \prod_{i=1}^n p_\beta(x_i)^{y_i}(1 - p_\beta(x_i))^{1-y_i}$$
:::



## Log-Likelihood

. . .

Taking the log and plugging in the expression of $p(x_i)$, we get the log-likelihood:

:::{style="font-size: 80%;"}
::: {.square-def}
$$\begin{aligned}
L(\beta, y_1, \ldots, y_n, x_1, \ldots, x_n) &= \ln(\ell) \\
&=\sum_{i=1}^n \left[y_i x_i^T \beta - \ln(1 + e^{x_i^T \beta})\right]
\end{aligned}$$
:::
:::

## MLE Calculation

. . .

If it exists, the MLE $\hat{\beta}$ is a zero of the gradient of $L$ with respect to $\beta$, which equals

::: {.square-def}
$$\frac{\partial L}{\partial \beta} = \sum_{i=1}^n x_i \left(y_i - \frac{e^{x_i^T \beta}}{1 + e^{x_i^T \beta}}\right)$$
:::



We must therefore solve a system of $p$ equations in $p$ unknowns.

. . .

There is no explicit solution: we use [numerical methods]{style="background-color: yellow;"} (Newton–Raphson algorithm).

## Remarks on Optimization

. . .

This is typical of advanced statistical models: we often [rely on optimization algorithms]{style="background-color: yellow;"}.

. . .

Two questions: does the solution exist? Is it unique?


## MLE Uniqueness

. . .

Let $X$ be the design matrix $(X^{(1)}, \dots, X^{(p)}) \in \mathbb R^{n \times p}$

. . .

::: {.callout-note}
## Proposition
If $\text{rank}(X) = p$, then the MLE, if it exists, is unique.
:::


## Proof of MLE Uniqueness

. . .

It suffices to show that [$L$ is strictly concave]{style="background-color: yellow;"} in $\beta$.

. . .

The Hessian matrix of $L$ is

$$\frac{\partial^2 L}{\partial \beta^2} = -\sum_{i=1}^n p_\beta(x_i)(1 - p_\beta(x_i)) x_i x_i^T$$

## Hessian Properties

. . .

It is [negative semi-definite]{style="background-color: yellow;"}. Moreover, for every $u \in \mathbb{R}^p$,

$$\begin{aligned}
u^T \frac{\partial^2 L}{\partial \beta^2} u = 0 &\Leftrightarrow u^T x_i x_i^T u = 0 \text{ for all } i\\
&\Leftrightarrow u^T x_i = 0 \text{ for all } i\\
&\Leftrightarrow Xu = 0\\
&\Leftrightarrow u = 0
\end{aligned}$$

where the last equivalence holds since [$\text{rank}(X) = p$]{style="background-color: lightblue;"}.

## Conclusion

. . .

Hence, for every $u \neq 0$,

::: {.square-def}
$$u^T \frac{\partial^2 L}{\partial \beta^2} u < 0$$
:::


The Hessian is negative definite, so $L$ is strictly concave.

Hence [the MLE, if it exists, is unique]{style="background-color: lightblue;"}.


## About MLE Existence

. . .

Even though $L$ is strictly concave, its [maximum can occur at infinity]{style="background-color: orange;"} (think of $t \mapsto -\ln(1+e^{-t})$, which increases towards $0$ without ever reaching it); then $\hat{\beta}$ does not exist.

. . .

This happens when there is [non-overlap]{style="background-color: yellow;"}, i.e. when a hyperplane separates the $x_i$ with $y_i = 0$ from those with $y_i = 1$.

## Non-Overlap Situation

. . .

Mathematically, there is [non-overlap]{style="background-color: yellow;"} if there exists [$\alpha \in \mathbb{R}^p$, $\alpha \neq 0$]{style="background-color: lightblue;"}, such that

$$\begin{cases}
\text{for all } i \text{ such that } y_i = 0, & \alpha^T x_i \geq 0 \\
\text{for all } i \text{ such that } y_i = 1, & \alpha^T x_i \leq 0
\end{cases}$$


## Illustration of Non-Overlap Situation {.smaller}

::: {style="font-size:90%"}
**Drag** a point across the boundary. Separated data: $\|\beta\|\to\infty$; gradient descent still converges *in direction*, to the max-margin separator.
:::

```{=html}
<div style="text-align:center">
  <canvas id="sepC" width="800" height="360" style="max-width:100%;background:#fff;border:1px solid #ddd;border-radius:8px;touch-action:none"></canvas>

  </div>
</div>
<script>
(function () {
  var cv=document.getElementById('sepC'); if(!cv||cv.dataset.init)return; cv.dataset.init=1;
  var c=cv.getContext('2d'),W=cv.width,H=cv.height,KEY='glmSep2';
  var kEl=document.getElementById('sepK'),kV=document.getElementById('sepKv'),playB=document.getElementById('sepPlay'),svmB=document.getElementById('sepSvm');
  var mBtns=[].slice.call(cv.parentNode.querySelectorAll('button[data-m]')),aBtns=[].slice.call(cv.parentNode.querySelectorAll('button[data-a]'));
  // left: data plane; right: ‖β‖ and angle to the max-margin direction along the iterations
  var PL=12,PT=12,PW=500,PH=336,SC=62.5,xr=PW/SC/2,yr=PH/SC/2;
  function X(x){return PL+PW/2+x*SC;} function Y(y){return PT+PH/2-y*SC;}
  function IX(px){return (px-PL-PW/2)/SC;} function IY(py){return (PT+PH/2-py)/SC;}
  function pos(e){var r=cv.getBoundingClientRect();return [(e.clientX-r.left)*W/r.width,(e.clientY-r.top)*H/r.height];}
  function gauss(){var u=0,v=0;while(!u)u=Math.random();while(!v)v=Math.random();return Math.sqrt(-2*Math.log(u))*Math.cos(2*Math.PI*v);}
  var NC=14,K=40,mode='sep',algo='newton',showSvm=true,pts=[],path=[],svm=null,TK=[];
  // gradient descents are shown at log-spaced iterations t_k = TMAX^(k/K), k = 0..K
  function setTK(){var TMAX=algo==='gd'?1e5:1e4;TK=[0];for(var k=1;k<=K;k++)TK.push(Math.max(TK[k-1]+1,Math.round(Math.pow(TMAX,k/K))));}
  function sig(t){return 1/(1+Math.exp(-t));}
  function l1pe(t){return t>0?t+Math.log1p(Math.exp(-t)):Math.log1p(Math.exp(t));}
  function eta(b,p){return b[0]+b[1]*p.x+b[2]*p.y;}
  function solve3(A,g){ // Gaussian elimination with partial pivoting
    var M=A.map(function(r,i){return r.concat([g[i]]);});
    for(var i=0;i<3;i++){var mx=i;for(var j=i+1;j<3;j++)if(Math.abs(M[j][i])>Math.abs(M[mx][i]))mx=j;var t=M[i];M[i]=M[mx];M[mx]=t;
      for(j=i+1;j<3;j++){var f=M[j][i]/M[i][i];for(var k=i;k<4;k++)M[j][k]-=f*M[i][k];}}
    var x=[0,0,0];for(i=2;i>=0;i--){var s=M[i][3];for(j=i+1;j<3;j++)s-=M[i][j]*x[j];x[i]=s/M[i][i];}return x;
  }
  function dev(b){var d=0;pts.forEach(function(p){var e=eta(b,p);d+=2*(p.c?l1pe(-e):l1pe(e));});return d;}
  function newton(){
    var b=[0,0,0];path=[b.slice()];
    for(var k=0;k<K;k++){
      var A=[[0,0,0],[0,0,0],[0,0,0]],g=[0,0,0];
      pts.forEach(function(p){var xi=[1,p.x,p.y],e=Math.max(-700,Math.min(700,eta(b,p))),sp=sig(e),sm=sig(-e),w=sp*sm,r=p.c?sm:-sp; // stable for |η| large
        for(var i=0;i<3;i++){g[i]+=r*xi[i];for(var j=0;j<3;j++)A[i][j]+=w*xi[i]*xi[j];}});
      var rg=1e-12*(A[0][0]+A[1][1]+A[2][2]);for(var ii=0;ii<3;ii++)A[ii][ii]+=rg;
      var s=solve3(A,g),n=Math.hypot(s[0],s[1],s[2]);if(!isFinite(n))break;

  function gd(kmax,norm){ // gradient ascent on the log-likelihood, step 4/tr(XᵀX); normalized: step divided by the loss
    var tr=0;pts.forEach(function(p){tr+=1+p.x*p.x+p.y*p.y;});
    var lr=4/tr,b0=0,b1=0,b2=0,t=0,n=pts.length,xs=pts.map(function(p){return p.x;}),ys=pts.map(function(p){return p.y;}),cs=pts.map(function(p){return p.c;});
    path=[[0,0,0]];

      for(;t<TK[k];t++){var g0=0,g1=0,g2=0;
        var Ls=0;
        for(var i=0;i<n;i++){var e=b0+b1*xs[i]+b2*ys[i],r=cs[i]?1/(1+Math.exp(e)):-1/(1+Math.exp(-e));g0+=r;g1+=r*xs[i];g2+=r*ys[i];if(norm)Ls+=cs[i]?l1pe(-e):l1pe(e);}

    function seg(p,a,b){var dx=b.x-a.x,dy=b.y-a.y,L=dx*dx+dy*dy,t=L?Math.max(0,Math.min(1,((p.x-a.x)*dx+(p.y-a.y)*dy)/L)):0;return {x:a.x+t*dx,y:a.y+t*dy};}
    function scan(S,T,flip){S.forEach(function(p){for(var i=0;i<T.length;i++)for(var j=i;j<T.length;j++){
      var q=seg(p,T[i],T[j]),d=Math.hypot(q.x-p.x,q.y-p.y);if(!best||d<best.d)best=flip?{d:d,a:q,b:p}:{d:d,a:p,b:q};}});}

  function hsvm(){

    c.strokeStyle='#2c3e50';c.beginPath();st=false;

  }

    sv.forEach(function(p){c.beginPath();c.arc(X(p.x),Y(p.y),11,0,7);c.strokeStyle='#8e44ad';c.lineWidth=2;c.stroke();});
    c.restore();c.lineWidth=1;
    c.strokeStyle='#ccc';c.strokeRect(PL,PT,PW,PH);
    c.font='13px sans-serif';c.textAlign='left';c.textBaseline='top';
    c.fillStyle='rgba(255,255,255,.85)';c.fillRect(PL+4,PT+PH-24,showSvm&&svm.ok?470:250,20);
    c.fillStyle='#2c3e50';c.fillText('— p = 0.5',PL+8,PT+PH-21);c.fillStyle='#666';c.fillText('- - p = 0.1, 0.9',PL+80,PT+PH-21);
    if(showSvm&&svm.ok){c.fillStyle='#8e44ad';c.fillText('- - max margin, SVM on (1, x, y)',PL+200,PT+PH-21);}

    var tx=PL+PW+16;
    c.font='13px sans-serif';c.textAlign='left';c.textBaseline='top';c.fillStyle='#333';
    c.fillText('‖β‖ = '+norms[k].toFixed(1)+'    deviance = '+dev(b).toFixed(3),tx,PT+282);
    if(svm.ok&&isFinite(angs[k]))c.fillText('angle to max margin = '+angs[k].toFixed(2)+'°',tx,PT+300);
    c.font='bold 13px sans-serif';c.fillStyle=svm.ok?'#c0392b':'#1e8449';
    c.fillText(svm.ok?'separated: the MLE does not exist':'overlap: the MLE exists, unique',tx,PT+322);
  }
  function save(){try{localStorage.setItem(KEY,JSON.stringify({m:mode,a:algo,s:showSvm,k:+kEl.value,p:pts}));}catch(e){}}
  var drag=-1,timer=null;
  function stop(){if(timer){clearInterval(timer);timer=null;playB.textContent='▶ run';}}
  cv.addEventListener('pointerdown',function(e){var p=pos(e),best=14;drag=-1;
    pts.forEach(function(q,i){var d=Math.hypot(X(q.x)-p[0],Y(q.y)-p[1]);if(d<best){best=d;drag=i;}});
    if(drag>=0){stop();cv.setPointerCapture(e.pointerId);e.preventDefault();}});
  cv.addEventListener('pointermove',function(e){if(drag<0)return;var p=pos(e);
    pts[drag].x=Math.max(-xr+.1,Math.min(xr-.1,IX(p[0])));pts[drag].y=Math.max(-yr+.1,Math.min(yr-.1,IY(p[1])));
    compute(true);draw();e.preventDefault();}); // GD: only up to t = 10⁴ while dragging
  window.addEventListener('pointerup',function(){if(drag>=0){drag=-1;compute();draw();save();}});
  function reset(){stop();compute();kEl.value=K;draw();save();}
  mBtns.forEach(function(bt){bt.onclick=function(){mode=bt.dataset.m;gen();reset();};});
  aBtns.forEach(function(bt){bt.onclick=function(){algo=bt.dataset.a;reset();};});
  svmB.onclick=function(){showSvm=!showSvm;draw();save();};
  document.getElementById('sepNew').onclick=function(){gen();reset();};
  kEl.addEventListener('input',function(){draw();save();});
  playB.onclick=function(){
    if(timer){stop();return;}
    kEl.value=0;draw();playB.textContent='■ stop';
    timer=setInterval(function(){var k=+kEl.value+1;if(k>K){stop();save();return;}kEl.value=k;draw();},180);
  };
  var sv=null;try{sv=JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem(KEY));}catch(e){}
  if(sv&&sv.p&&sv.p.length===2*NC){mode=sv.m==='ovl'?'ovl':'sep';algo=(sv.a==='gd'||sv.a==='ngd')?sv.a:'newton';showSvm=sv.s!==false;pts=sv.p;compute();kEl.value=sv.k;}else gen();
  draw();save();
})();
</script>
```


## Non-Overlap and Existence

. . .

::: {.callout-note}
## Proposition (admitted)
In case of non-overlap, [$\hat{\beta}$ does not exist]{style="background-color: orange;"}: $L(\beta)$ is maximal only as $\|\beta\| \to \infty$ (in one or several directions).
:::

. . .

As $\|\beta\| \to \infty$ along a separating direction, [$p_\beta(x) \to 0$ or $1$]{style="background-color: lightblue;"} for every $x$ off the hyperplane, depending on its side.

. . .

However, there is a "dead zone" between the $2$ point clouds, because the [separating hyperplane is not necessarily unique]{style="background-color: orange;"}.

## Beyond the Dead Zone

. . .

Outside this dead zone, classification is trivial ($0$ or $1$).

. . .

But the model cannot be interpreted: the ORs are $0$ or $+\infty$.


## Existence and Uniqueness of MLE

. . .

We say that [there is overlap]{style="background-color: yellow;"} when no hyperplane separates the red points from the blue points (the $x_i$ with $y_i = 0$ from those with $y_i = 1$).

. . .

::: {.callout-note}
## Proposition (admitted)
If $\text{rank}(X) = p$ and [there is overlap]{style="background-color: yellow;"}, then the MLE exists and is unique.
:::


Under these conditions, we [can safely search for the MLE]{style="background-color: yellow;"} with the Newton–Raphson algorithm, since:


1. the maximum exists,


2. the function to optimize is strictly concave, so it has no local maximum other than the global one.


## Fisher Information (Recall)

. . .

Let $X$ be the design matrix (whose rows are the vectors $x_i$).

. . .

We denote by $J_n(\beta)$ the Fisher information matrix:

::: {.square-def}
$$J_n(\beta) = -E\left[\frac{\partial^2 L}{\partial \beta^2}(\beta) \bigg| X\right]$$
:::



## Asymptotic Normality of the MLE



::: {.callout-note}
## Proposition (admitted)
In the logistic regression model, [if]{style="background-color: yellow;"}

1. the distribution of the regressors $(X^{(1)}, \ldots, X^{(p)})$ has compact support,
2. $\text{rank}(X) = p$,
3. the smallest eigenvalue of $X^T X$ tends to infinity with $n$,

[then]{style="background-color: yellow;"}

1. the maximum likelihood estimator $\hat{\beta}$ is consistent;

2. $J_n(\beta)^{1/2}(\hat{\beta} - \beta) \xrightarrow{L} N(0, I_p)$

where $I_p$ is the identity matrix of size $p$.
:::


## Comments

. . .

Under these conditions, [the MLE exists for $n$ large enough]{style="background-color: lightblue;"}: the probability of overlap tends to $1$ as $n \to \infty$.

. . .

The MLE is asymptotically efficient (minimal asymptotic variance).

. . .

We can rely on [asymptotic normality]{style="background-color: yellow;"} to build tests and confidence intervals.

## Comparison: Linear Regression

. . .

The formula for $\hat{\beta}$ is [explicit]{style="background-color: lightgreen;"}: $\hat{\beta} = (X^T X)^{-1} X^T Y$;

. . .

Its expectation and variance are [explicit]{style="background-color: lightgreen;"};

. . .

In the Gaussian model ($Y|X$ Gaussian), the distribution of $\hat{\beta}$ is [explicit]{style="background-color: lightgreen;"}, which gives exact tests (Student, Fisher).

. . .

Without the Gaussian assumption, these tests are only asymptotically valid.

## Comparison: Logistic Regression

. . .

[No explicit]{style="background-color: orange;"} formula for $\hat{\beta}$: it is computed numerically;

. . .

We know neither the bias nor the variance of $\hat{\beta}$;

. . .

The distribution of $Y|X$ is simple (a Bernoulli), but the exact distribution of $\hat{\beta}$ is unknown.

. . .

We only know its asymptotic distribution.

. . .

Hence we use [asymptotic tests]{style="background-color: orange;"}!


# Wald Tests and Confidence Intervals

## Outline: Inference

- **Wald tests** and confidence intervals, from the asymptotic normality of $\hat\beta$: one coefficient, one odds ratio
- **Deviance**: how far a model is from the saturated model
- **Deviance tests** (likelihood ratio tests) for nested models; AIC and BIC

## Asymptotic Framework

. . .

Under "good conditions" (see the proposition above),

::: {.square-def}
$$J_n(\beta)^{1/2}(\hat{\beta} - \beta) \xrightarrow{L} N(0, I_p)$$
:::

where $J_n(\beta)$ is the Fisher information matrix.

. . .

To build asymptotic tests, we need [an expression for $J_n(\beta)$]{style="background-color: yellow;"} and [a way to estimate it]{style="background-color: yellow;"} ($\beta$ is unknown).


## Computation of Jₙ(β)

. . .

::: {.square-def}
$$J_n(\beta) = -E\left[\frac{\partial^2 L}{\partial \beta^2}(\beta) \bigg| X\right]$$
:::



where $L$ is the log-likelihood of the model.

. . .

Using the Hessian computed in the uniqueness proof,

::: {.square-def}
$$J_n(\beta) = \sum_{i=1}^n p_\beta(x_i)(1 - p_\beta(x_i)) x_i x_i^T$$
:::

## Equivalent Form

. . .

Equivalently,

::: {.square-def}
$$J_n(\beta) = X^T W_\beta X$$
:::



where $X$ is the design matrix and $W_\beta$ is the diagonal matrix

. . .

:::{style="font-size: 60%;"}
::: {.square-def}
$$W_\beta = \begin{pmatrix}
p_\beta(x_1)(1 - p_\beta(x_1)) & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\
0 & p_\beta(x_2)(1 - p_\beta(x_2)) & \cdots & 0 \\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
0 & 0 & \cdots & p_\beta(x_n)(1 - p_\beta(x_n))
\end{pmatrix}$$
:::


:::

## Estimating the Information Matrix

. . .

To estimate $J_n(\beta)$, we simply replace $\beta$ by the MLE $\hat{\beta}$.

. . .

Under the same regularity assumptions, we can show that

::: {.square-def}
$$J_n(\hat{\beta})^{1/2}(\hat{\beta} - \beta) \xrightarrow{L} N(0, I_p)$$
:::

## Estimated Variance of β̂ⱼ

. . .

::: {.square-def}
$$J_n(\hat{\beta})^{1/2}(\hat{\beta} - \beta) \xrightarrow{L} N(0, I_p)$$
:::



. . .

Denote by [$\hat{\sigma}_j^2$]{style="background-color: lightblue;"} the $j$-th diagonal element of [$J_n(\hat{\beta})^{-1}$]{style="background-color: lightblue;"}. Then (admitted):

::: {.square-def}
$$\frac{\hat{\beta}_j - \beta_j}{\hat{\sigma}_j} \xrightarrow{L} N(0, 1)$$
:::



## Confidence Interval

. . .

This yields a confidence interval for $\beta_j$ at asymptotic confidence level $1 - \alpha$:

::: {.square-def}
$$\text{CI}_{1-\alpha}(\beta_j) = \left[\hat{\beta}_j - q_{1-\alpha/2}\hat{\sigma}_j \,;\, \hat{\beta}_j + q_{1-\alpha/2}\hat{\sigma}_j\right]$$

:::


where $q_{1-\alpha/2}$ is the quantile of order $1 - \alpha/2$ of the $N(0, 1)$ distribution.

. . .

One can check that [$\P(\beta_j \in \text{CI}_{1-\alpha}(\beta_j)) \to 1 - \alpha$]{style="background-color: lightblue;"}.


## Significance Test for One Coefficient

. . .

We want to test [$H_0: \beta_j = 0$ against $H_1: \beta_j \neq 0$]{style="background-color: yellow;"}.


Under $H_0$, [$\frac{\hat{\beta}_j}{\hat{\sigma}_j} \xrightarrow{L} N(0, 1)$]{style="background-color: lightblue;"}



This gives a critical region at asymptotic level $\alpha$:

::: {.square-def}
$$\mathcal R_\alpha = \left\{\frac{|\hat{\beta}_j|}{\hat{\sigma}_j} > q_{1-\alpha/2}\right\}$$
:::



. . .

Indeed $P_{H_0}(\mathcal R_\alpha) \to \alpha$.

This is the [Wald test]{style="background-color: yellow;"} (based on the asymptotic normality of the MLE).

## P-value

. . .

With $\Phi$ the cdf of the $\mathcal N(0, 1)$ distribution, the p-value of the test is

::: {.square-def}
$$p\text{-value} = 2\left(1 - \Phi\left(\frac{|\hat{\beta}_j|}{\hat{\sigma}_j}\right)\right)$$
:::



## Example in R

. . .

:::{style="font-size: 50%;"}
| Variable    | Estimate   | Std. Error | z value | Pr(>|z|)    | Significance |
|-------------|------------|------------|---------|-------------|--------------|
| (Intercept) | -3.9564361 | 0.3155529  | -12.538 | < 2e-16     | ***          |
| AGE         | 0.0640837  | 0.0123960  | 5.170   | 2.34e-07    | ***          |
| I(AGE^2)    | -0.0006758 | 0.0001260  | -5.364  | 8.14e-08    | ***          |
| DBP         | 0.0121546  | 0.0033775  | 3.599   | 0.00032     | ***          |
| SEXEFEMME   | 0.5155651  | 0.0776229  | 6.642   | 3.10e-11    | ***          |
| WALK1       | -0.4042257 | 0.0913195  | -4.426  | 9.58e-06    | ***          |
| ACTIV1      | -0.6573558 | 0.1150226  | -5.715  | 1.10e-08    | ***          |
:::


. . .

The first three columns give, respectively:

::: {.nonincremental}
- $\hat \beta_j$
- $\hat \sigma_j$
- $\hat \beta_j/\hat \sigma_j$ (z-score).
:::


## Estimation of an Odds-Ratio

. . .

Consider two individuals $1$ and $2$ who differ only in regressor $j$. Then

::: {.square-def}

$$OR(x_1^{(j)}, x_2^{(j)}) = e^{\beta_j(x_1^{(j)} - x_2^{(j)})}$$
:::



. . .

**Question**: do we have $OR(x_1^{(j)}, x_2^{(j)})\approx 1$?

. . .

The OR is simply estimated by

::: {.square-def}
$$\widehat{OR}(x_1^{(j)}, x_2^{(j)}) = e^{\hat{\beta}_j(x_1^{(j)} - x_2^{(j)})}$$
:::



## Important Example

. . .

If regressor $j$ is binary with $x_1^{(j)} = 1$ and $x_2^{(j)} = 0$, then

::: {.square-def}
$$\widehat{OR}(x_1^{(j)}, x_2^{(j)}) = e^{\hat{\beta}_j}$$
:::

## Asymptotic CI for an Odds-Ratio

. . .

We have seen that an asymptotic CI at confidence level $1 - \alpha$ for ${\beta}_j$ is

::: {.square-def}
$$\text{CI}_{1-\alpha}(\beta_j) = \left[\hat{\beta}_j - q_{1-\alpha/2}\hat{\sigma}_j \,;\, \hat{\beta}_j + q_{1-\alpha/2}\hat{\sigma}_j\right]= [l,r]$$
:::



. . .

If $x_1^{(j)} > x_2^{(j)}$, an asymptotic CI for $OR(x_1^{(j)}, x_2^{(j)})= e^{\beta_j(x^{(j)}_1 - x^{(j)}_2)}$ at level $1 - \alpha$ is

::: {.square-def}
$$\text{CI}_{1-\alpha}(OR(x_1^{(j)}, x_2^{(j)})) = \left[e^{l(x_1^{(j)} - x_2^{(j)})}, e^{r(x_1^{(j)} - x_2^{(j)})}\right]$$
:::


## Significance Test for an Odds-Ratio

. . .

We usually want to compare $OR(x_1^{(j)}, x_2^{(j)})$ with $1$:

::: {.square-def}
$$OR(x_1^{(j)}, x_2^{(j)}) = 1 \Leftrightarrow e^{\beta_j(x_1^{(j)} - x_2^{(j)})} = 1 \Leftrightarrow \beta_j = 0$$
:::



## Two-Sided Test

. . .

::: {.square-def}
$H_0: OR(x_1^{(j)}, x_2^{(j)}) = 1$ VS $H_1: OR(x_1^{(j)}, x_2^{(j)}) \neq 1$
:::

. . .

amounts to testing [$H_0: \beta_j = 0$ against $H_1: \beta_j \neq 0$]{style="background-color: lightblue;"}. The rejection region at asymptotic level $\alpha$ is

. . .

::: {.square-def}
$$\mathcal R_\alpha = \left\{\frac{|\hat{\beta}_j|}{\hat{\sigma}_j} > q_{1-\alpha/2}\right\}$$
:::



## One-Sided Tests

. . .

However, for ORs, one [often prefers one-sided tests]{style="background-color: yellow;"}, e.g.

. . .

::: {.square-def}
$H_0: OR(x_1^{(j)}, x_2^{(j)}) = 1$ VS $H_1: OR(x_1^{(j)}, x_2^{(j)}) > 1$
:::



. . .

If $x_1^{(j)} > x_2^{(j)}$, then [$OR(x_1^{(j)}, x_2^{(j)}) \geq 1 \Leftrightarrow \beta_j \geq 0$]{style="background-color: lightblue;"}, so the rejection region at asymptotic level $\alpha$ is

::: {.square-def}
$$\mathcal R_{\alpha}=\left\{\frac{\hat{\beta}_j}{\hat{\sigma}_j} > q_{1-\alpha}\right\}$$
:::



# Deviance


## Saturated Model

. . .

Suppose we have $n$ observations $(Y_1, \dots, Y_n)$ and $(X_1, \dots, X_n)$, with categorical regressors.

. . .

Here $X_k$ may be a vector $X_k = (X^{(1)}_k, \dots, X^{(p)}_k)^T$. 

. . .


Assume that the individuals are i.i.d., with [$\mathbb P(Y=1|X_k=x) = p(x)$]{style="background-color: lightblue;"}.

. . .

How do we estimate $p(x)$?

## Saturated Estimator

. . .

Suppose we have $n$ observations $(Y_1, \dots, Y_n)$ and $(X_1, \dots, X_n)$

. . .

[$n(x) = |\{k:~ X_k = x\}|$]{style="background-color: lightblue;"} (number of individuals $k$ with $X_k=x$)

. . .

[$n_1(x) = |\{k:~ X_k = x ~~\text{and}~~Y_k=1\}|$ ]{style="background-color: lightblue;"}

. . .

The [saturated model]{style="background-color: yellow;"} estimates $p(x)$, for each observed $x$, by

::: {.square-def}
$$\hat{p}_{\text{sat}}(x) = \frac{n_1(x)}{n(x)}$$
:::



## Saturated Estimator: Illustration {.smaller}

::: {style="font-size:90%"}
Few distinct values of $x$: $\hat p_{\text{sat}}(x)=n_1(x)/n(x)$ is close to $p(x)$. All values distinct: it is $0$ or $1$. The **nearest neighbour** rule extends it to every $x$.
:::

```{=html}
<div style="text-align:center">
  <canvas id="satC" width="720" height="300" style="max-width:100%;background:#fff;border:1px solid #ddd;border-radius:8px"></canvas>
  <div class="lm-row">
    distinct values of x:
    <button class="lm-btn" data-l="4">4</button>
    <button class="lm-btn" data-l="8">8</button>
    <button class="lm-btn" data-l="20">20</button>
    <button class="lm-btn" data-l="0">all distinct</button>
    &nbsp; <button class="lm-btn" id="satNN">nearest neighbour</button>
    <button class="lm-btn" id="satNew">↻ resample</button>
  </div>
</div>
<script>
(function () {
  var cv=document.getElementById('satC'); if(!cv||cv.dataset.init)return; cv.dataset.init=1;
  var c=cv.getContext('2d'),W=cv.width,H=cv.height,KEY='glmSat';
  var lBtns=[].slice.call(cv.parentNode.querySelectorAll('button[data-l]')),nnB=document.getElementById('satNN');
  var n=40,ux=[],uu=[],L=8,nn=false;
  var ml=52,mr=16,mt=14,mb=40,x0=-.3,x1=10.3,y0=-.12,y1=1.12;
  function X(x){return ml+(x-x0)/(x1-x0)*(W-ml-mr);} function Y(p){return H-mb-(p-y0)/(y1-y0)*(H-mt-mb);}
  function ptrue(x){return 1/(1+Math.exp(-(-3+0.6*x)));}
  function base(){for(var i=0;i<n;i++){ux[i]=Math.random();uu[i]=Math.random();}}
  function draw(){
    lBtns.forEach(function(b){b.classList.toggle('on',+b.dataset.l===L);});nnB.classList.toggle('on',nn);
    // data: x on L equally spaced levels (or continuous), y ~ B(p(x)) from fixed uniforms
    var xs=[],ys=[];
    for(var i=0;i<n;i++){var x=L?10*Math.min(L-1,Math.floor(ux[i]*L))/(L-1):10*ux[i];xs.push(x);ys.push(uu[i]<ptrue(x)?1:0);}
    var g={};xs.forEach(function(x,i){var k=x.toFixed(6);g[k]=g[k]||{x:x,n:0,n1:0,k:0};g[k].n++;g[k].n1+=ys[i];});
    var lv=Object.keys(g).map(function(k){return g[k];}).sort(function(a,b){return a.x-b.x;});
    c.clearRect(0,0,W,H);c.fillStyle='#fff';c.fillRect(0,0,W,H);c.lineWidth=1;c.font='13px sans-serif';
    c.fillStyle='#666';c.textAlign='right';c.textBaseline='middle';
    [0,.5,1].forEach(function(p){c.strokeStyle=p===.5?'#eee':'#ccc';c.beginPath();c.moveTo(ml,Y(p));c.lineTo(W-mr,Y(p));c.stroke();c.fillText(p,ml-8,Y(p));});
    c.textAlign='center';c.textBaseline='top';for(var t=0;t<=10;t+=2)c.fillText(t,X(t),H-mb+5);
    c.fillStyle='#333';c.fillText('x',(ml+W-mr)/2,H-mb+20);
    // true p(x)
    c.strokeStyle='#999';c.lineWidth=2;c.setLineDash([6,5]);c.beginPath();
    for(var j=0;j<=200;j++){var xx=x0+(x1-x0)*j/200;j?c.lineTo(X(xx),Y(ptrue(xx))):c.moveTo(X(xx),Y(ptrue(xx)));}c.stroke();c.setLineDash([]);
    // nearest neighbour: step function through the saturated values
    if(nn){
      c.strokeStyle='#e67e22';c.lineWidth=2;c.beginPath();
      lv.forEach(function(v,i){var a=i?(lv[i-1].x+v.x)/2:x0,b=i<lv.length-1?(v.x+lv[i+1].x)/2:x1,p=v.n1/v.n;
        if(i)c.lineTo(X(a),Y(p));else c.moveTo(X(a),Y(p));c.lineTo(X(b),Y(p));});
      c.stroke();
    }
    // data points, stacked outward from 0 and 1
    var stk={},cnt={};xs.forEach(function(x,i){var k=x.toFixed(6)+'_'+ys[i];cnt[k]=(cnt[k]||0)+1;stk.max=Math.max(stk.max||0,cnt[k]-1);});
    xs.forEach(function(x,i){var k=x.toFixed(6)+'_'+ys[i];stk[k]=(stk[k]||0)+1;var s=stk[k]-1;
      var sp=Math.min(6,28/Math.max(1,stk.max||1));c.beginPath();c.arc(X(x),ys[i]?Y(1)-s*sp:Y(0)+s*sp,3.4,0,7);c.fillStyle='rgba(44,62,80,.6)';c.fill();});
    // saturated estimator at each observed x
    lv.forEach(function(v){var p=v.n1/v.n;
      c.beginPath();c.arc(X(v.x),Y(p),L&&L<=8?7:5,0,7);c.fillStyle='#e67e22';c.fill();c.strokeStyle='#fff';c.lineWidth=1.5;c.stroke();
      if(L&&L<=8){c.fillStyle='#b9651e';c.font='12px sans-serif';c.textAlign='left';c.textBaseline='middle';c.fillText(v.n1+'/'+v.n,X(v.x)+10,Y(p)-(p>.85?-12:10));}});
    c.lineWidth=1;
    // legend
    c.font='13px sans-serif';c.textAlign='left';c.textBaseline='middle';
    c.strokeStyle='#999';c.lineWidth=2;c.setLineDash([6,5]);c.beginPath();c.moveTo(X(0),Y(.9));c.lineTo(X(.6),Y(.9));c.stroke();c.setLineDash([]);
    c.fillStyle='#333';c.fillText('true p(x)',X(.75),Y(.9));
    c.beginPath();c.arc(X(.3),Y(.78),5,0,7);c.fillStyle='#e67e22';c.fill();
    c.fillStyle='#333';c.fillText('saturated estimate  n₁(x)/n(x)'+(nn?'   — nearest neighbour':''),X(.75),Y(.78));
    c.textAlign='right';c.fillStyle='#555';
    c.fillText('n = '+n+',  '+lv.length+' distinct x,  about '+(n/lv.length).toFixed(1)+' obs. per x',W-mr-8,Y(.5)+14);
    c.lineWidth=1;
    try{localStorage.setItem(KEY,JSON.stringify({l:L,nn:nn}));}catch(e){}
  }
  lBtns.forEach(function(b){b.onclick=function(){L=+b.dataset.l;draw();};});
  nnB.onclick=function(){nn=!nn;draw();};
  document.getElementById('satNew').onclick=function(){base();draw();};
  base();
  try{var sv=JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem(KEY));if(sv){L=[0,4,8,20].indexOf(sv.l)>=0?sv.l:8;nn=!!sv.nn;}}catch(e){}
  draw();
})();
</script>
```

## Remark: Distinct Observations

. . .

::: {.square-def}
$$\hat{p}_{\text{sat}}(x) = \frac{n_1(x)}{n(x)}$$
:::

[If all observations are distinct]{style="background-color: yellow;"}, i.e. each observed $x$ corresponds to a single individual, then for every observed $x$:

. . .

$n(x) = 1$, $n_1(x) \in \{0,1\}$, and $\hat{p}_{\text{sat}}(x) = 0$ or $1$.


## Properties of the Saturated Model

. . .

The saturated model is the [most flexible model]{style="background-color: yellow;"}: one parameter per distinct value of $x$.

. . .

It fits the data perfectly.

. . .

However, it has [no explanatory power]{style="background-color: orange;"} (what is the effect of the regressors on $Y$?).

. . .

Nor does it say anything about $p(x)$ for an unobserved $x$.

. . .

It serves as a [reference]{style="background-color: yellow;"} to assess the fit of other models.


## Likelihood of Saturated Estimator

. . .

Given probabilities $p(x)$, the log-likelihood is

:::{style="font-size: 80%;"}
::: {.square-def}
$$L(y_1, \ldots, y_n|x_1, \ldots, x_n) = \sum_{i=1}^n y_i \ln(p(x_i)) + (1 - y_i) \ln(1 - p(x_i))$$
:::
:::

. . .

The saturated estimator maximizes this log-likelihood over all choices of $p(x)$; we denote

:::{style="font-size: 80%;"}
::: {.square-def}
$$L_{\text{sat}} = \sum_{i=1}^n y_i \ln(\hat p_{\text{sat}}(x_i)) + (1 - y_i) \ln(1 - \hat p_{\text{sat}}(x_i))$$
:::
:::


## Case 1: Distinct Observations

. . .

If all observations $x_i$ are distinct, we have $\hat{p}_{\text{sat}}(x_i) = y_i$ with $y_i \in \{0, 1\}$, hence

::: {.square-def}
$$L_{\text{sat}} = 0$$
:::



. . .

This is the highest possible log-likelihood: the saturated estimator [fits the data perfectly]{style="background-color: orange;"} (too well).

## Case 2: Non-Distinct Observations

. . .

If the observations [$x_i$ are not distinct]{style="background-color: yellow;"}, we obtain

:::{style="font-size: 80%;"}
::: {.square-def}

$$L_{\text{sat}} = \sum_x \left[n_1(x) \ln\left(\frac{n_1(x)}{n(x)}\right) + (n(x) - n_1(x)) \ln\left(1 - \frac{n_1(x)}{n(x)}\right)\right]$$
:::


:::

where the sum runs over the distinct values $x$ taken by the $x_i$.



## Deviance

. . .

The deviance of a model measures how much it [deviates from the saturated model]{style="background-color: yellow;"} (the best possible model in terms of likelihood).

. . .

::: {.square-def}
$$D = 2(L_{\text{sat}} - L_{\text{mod}})$$
:::


where $L_{\text{mod}}$ is the maximized log-likelihood of the model.

. . .

We always have [$D \geq 0$]{style="background-color: lightblue;"}.

. . .

If all observations are distinct, $L_{\text{sat}} = 0$, hence [$D = -2L_{\text{mod}}$]{style="background-color: lightblue;"}

## Role of Deviance and Computation in R

. . .

::: {.square-def}
$$D = 2(L_{\text{sat}} - L_{\text{mod}})$$
:::

. . .

Deviance plays the role of the SSR of a linear model: [the higher the deviance, the worse the model fits]{style="background-color: yellow;"} the data.

. . .

With 0/1 responses (one row per individual), R takes $L_{\text{sat}} = 0$: the reported deviance is [$-2L_{\text{mod}}$]{style="background-color: orange;"}.


# Deviance Tests and Model Selection

## Linear Constraint Test

. . .

As in linear regression, we want to test [$H_0: R\beta = 0$ VS $H_1: R\beta \neq 0$]{style="background-color: lightblue;"}

where $R$ is a full-rank constraint matrix of size [$(q, p)$]{style="background-color: lightblue;"}.



. . .

Recall that, depending on the choice of $R$, this covers:


- the global test: is there at least one relevant regressor?


- comparing nested models


- the joint significance of a group of regressors

## Available Procedures

. . .

In GLMs, three test procedures address this problem.



**The Wald test**, based on the asymptotic normality of $\hat{\beta}$, generalizing the test of $\beta_j = 0$ against $\beta_j \neq 0$ seen earlier.

. . .

[**The likelihood ratio test**]{style="background-color: yellow;"}, called in this context the [deviance test]{style="background-color: yellow;"}.

. . .

**The score test**, based on the gradient of the log-likelihood at the MLE under $H_0$, $\hat{\beta}_{H_0}$.

. . .

**Most used**: the [deviance test]{style="background-color: yellow;"}.


## The Deviance Test (or Likelihood Ratio Test)

. . .

To test [ $H_0: R\beta = 0$ against $H_1: R\beta \neq 0$]{style="background-color: lightblue;"}, the principle is as follows.

. . .

Compute the MLE in each model: $\hat{\beta}$ in the full model and [$\hat{\beta}_{H_0}$ in the constrained model]{style="background-color: yellow;"}.

. . .

**Logic**: If $H_0$ is true, the constrained model should be as "likely" as the full model, so [$L(\hat{\beta})$ and $L(\hat{\beta}_{H_0})$ should be similar]{style="background-color: yellow;"}.

## Deviance Test Statistic

. . .

The test statistic is the [difference of deviances]{style="background-color: yellow;"}:

::: {.square-def}
$$D_{H_0} - D_{H_1} = 2\left(L(\hat{\beta}) - L(\hat{\beta}_{H_0})\right)$$
:::

. . .

Under $H_0$, with $q$ the number of constraints, we have (admitted):

::: {.square-def}
$$D_{H_0} - D_{H_1} = 2\left(L(\hat{\beta}) - L(\hat{\beta}_{H_0})\right) \xrightarrow{L} \chi^2_q$$
:::



## Rejection Region and P-value

. . .

The rejection region at asymptotic level $\alpha$ is therefore

::: {.square-def}
$$\mathcal R_\alpha = \{D_{H_0} - D_{H_1} > \chi^2_{q,1-\alpha}\}$$
:::



where $\chi^2_{q,1-\alpha}$ is the quantile of order $1 - \alpha$ of the $\chi^2_q$ distribution.


. . .

The p-value is

::: {.square-def}

$$p\text{-value} = 1 - F(D_{H_0} - D_{H_1})$$
:::



where $F$ is the cdf of a $\chi^2_q$ distribution.


## Special Case 1: Significance Test

. . .

We want to test whether a model (with a constant) is significant.

. . .

We test $H_0$: all [coefficients are zero except the constant]{style="background-color: yellow;"}, i.e. the special case

::: {.square-def}
$R = [0 | I_{p-1}]$.
:::



. . .

We [compare the deviance of the model to the null deviance $D_0$]{style="background-color: yellow;"}, the deviance of the model containing only the constant.

## Test Statistic

. . .

The test statistic is $D_0 - D$. Under $H_0$, when $n \to \infty$:

::: {.square-def}
$$D_0 - D \sim \chi^2_{p-1}$$
:::

. . .

The model is [declared significant]{style="background-color: yellow;"} (relative to the null model) if the sample falls in the critical region of asymptotic level $\alpha$:

::: {.square-def}
$$\mathcal R_\alpha = \{D_0 - D > \chi^2_{p-1,1-\alpha}\}$$
:::


## Special Case 2: Nested Models

. . .


Suppose that model [$1$ (with deviance $D_1$) is a sub-model of model $2$]{style="background-color: yellow;"} (with deviance $D_2$)

. . .

Model $1$ is then obtained from model $2$ (parameter $\beta$) through a constraint $R\beta = 0$, where [$R$ is a $(q, p)$ matrix]{style="background-color: lightblue;"}.


. . .

Under $H_0: R\beta = 0$, we have asymptotically [$D_1 - D_2 \sim \chi^2_q$]{style="background-color: lightblue;"}

. . .


Hence the asymptotic test:

::: {.square-def}
$\mathcal R_\alpha = \{D_1 - D_2 > \chi^2_{q,1 - \alpha}\}$

:::


## AIC and BIC Criteria

. . .

AIC and BIC are defined as in linear regression:

::: {.square-def}
$\text{AIC} = -2L_{\text{mod}} + 2p$
:::

::: {.square-def}
$\text{BIC} = -2L_{\text{mod}} + \ln(n)p$
:::



where $L_{\text{mod}}$ is the maximized log-likelihood of the fitted model.

## AIC and BIC via Deviance

. . .

If we ignore the saturated likelihood, i.e. set $L_{\text{sat}}=0$,

::: {.square-def}
$\text{AIC} = D + 2p$
:::

::: {.square-def}
$\text{BIC} = D + \ln(n)p$
:::


**In practice**, we choose the model with the [smallest AIC or BIC]{style="background-color: yellow;"}.

. . .

As in linear regression, we can use automatic selection procedures (backward, forward, etc.).

## Example: Obesity Study

. . .

```r
model=glm(Y~AGE+DBP+SEXE+ACTIV+WALK+MARITAL, family=binomial)
summary(model)
```

. . .


:::{style="font-size: 60%;"}
| Statistic | Value | Degrees of Freedom |
|-----------|-------|-------------------|
| Null deviance | $4610.8$ | on $5300$ |
| Residual deviance | $4459.5$ | on $5290$ |
| AIC | $4481.5$ | |
:::

. . .

The model deviance is $D = 4459.5$.

**Significance test**: we compare $D$ to the null deviance $D_0 = 4610.8$: [$D_0 - D = 151.3$]{style="background-color: lightblue;"}. The p-value of the test is [$1 - F_{10}(151.3) \approx 0$]{style="background-color: lightblue;"} where $F_{10}$ is the cdf of a $\chi^2_{10}$.

. . .

[The model is significant]{style="background-color: lightgreen;"}.


## Example: Significance Test of MARITAL

. . .



```r
model=glm(Y~AGE+DBP+SEXE+ACTIV+WALK, family=binomial) # We want to test if `MARITAL` is significant
summary(model)
```

. . .

:::{style="font-size: 60%;"}
| Statistic | Value | Degrees of Freedom |
|-----------|-------|-------------------|
| Null deviance | $4610.8$ | on $5300$ |
| Residual deviance | $4462.7$ | on $5295$ |
| AIC | $4474.7$ | |
:::

. . .

The deviance is now $D_2 = 4462.7$. Compared with the previous model: [$D_2 - D = 3.2$]{style="background-color: lightblue;"}.

. . .

The p-value of the test is [$1 - F_5(3.2) \approx 0.67$]{style="background-color: lightblue;"}, where $F_5$ is the cdf of the $\chi^2_5$ distribution.


We therefore [do not reject $H_0$]{style="background-color: yellow;"}: the [MARITAL coefficients can be taken to be zero]{style="background-color: yellow;"} (the AIC confirms it).

## Example: Significance Test of AGE²

. . .

```r
model=glm(Y~AGE+I(AGE^2)+DBP+SEXE+WALK+ACTIV, family=binomial) # We add AGE^2
summary(model)
```

:::{style="font-size: 60%;"}
| Statistic | Value | Degrees of Freedom |
|-----------|-------|-------------------|
| Null deviance | $4610.8$ | on $5300$ |
| Residual deviance | $4439.5$ | on $5294$ |
| AIC | $4453.5$ | |
:::

. . .

The deviance test against the previous model has p-value [$1 - F_1(4462.7 - 4439.5) = 1 - F_1(23.2) \approx 10^{-6}$]{style="background-color: lightblue;"}

. . .

This model is [therefore preferable]{style="background-color: yellow;"} (the AIC confirms it).

. . .

However, we [cannot compare this model with the first one]{style="background-color: orange;"} by a deviance test, since they are [not nested]{style="background-color: orange;"}.

. . .

We [can still compare their AICs]{style="background-color: lightgreen;"}: this model is preferable.


# Prediction

## Setting and Objective

. . .

Suppose we are interested in a [new individual]{style="background-color: yellow;"} for whom

- we know their characteristics $x \in \mathbb{R}^p$,
- we do not know their $Y$.

. . .

**Goal**: [predict $Y$]{style="background-color: yellow;"} for this new individual.

## Recall in the Logit Model

. . .

Once we have [fitted a logistic regression]{style="background-color: yellow;"} model, we estimate

::: {.square-def}
$$p_\beta(x) = P(Y = 1|X = x)$$
:::



by

. . .

::: {.square-def}
$$p_{\hat{\beta}}(x) = \text{logit}^{-1}(x^T \hat{\beta}) = \frac{e^{x^T \hat{\beta}}}{1 + e^{x^T \hat{\beta}}}$$
:::



## Outline for Prediction

. . .

::: {.square-def}
$$p_\beta(x) = P(Y = 1|X = x)$$
:::

We will see:


1. how to construct a [confidence interval around the estimate $p_{\hat{\beta}}(x)$]{style="background-color: yellow;"};


2. how to use this estimate to [classify the new individual]{style="background-color: yellow;"} in category $Y = 0$ or $Y = 1$.

## CI: Asymptotic Distribution of β̂

. . .

We know that, for large $n$ (when $n \to \infty$):

::: {.square-def}
$$\hat{\beta} \sim N(\beta, (X^T W_{\hat{\beta}} X)^{-1})$$
:::

- $X=(X^{(1)}, \dots, X^{(p)})$ is the $n \times p$ [design matrix]{style="background-color: yellow;"}
- $W_{\hat{\beta}}$ is the $n \times n$ [diagonal matrix]{style="background-color: yellow;"} with diagonal entries [$p_{\hat \beta}(x_i)(1-p_{\hat \beta}(x_i))$]{style="background-color: lightblue;"}


## CI for Linear Predictor

. . .

Hence, when $n \to +\infty$, [$x^T \hat{\beta} \sim N(x^T \beta, x^T (X^T W_{\hat{\beta}} X)^{-1} x)$ ]{style="background-color: lightblue;"}, which gives the asymptotic CI for $x^T\beta$:

. . .

::: {.square-def}
$$\text{CI}_{1-\alpha}(x^T \beta) = \left[x^T \hat{\beta} \pm q_{1-\alpha/2} \sqrt{x^T (X^T W_{\hat{\beta}} X)^{-1} x}\right]$$
:::



## CI for Probability pβ(x)

. . .

Since [$p_{\hat{\beta}}(x) = \text{logit}^{-1}(x^T \hat{\beta})$]{style="background-color: lightblue;"} and $\text{logit}^{-1}$ is increasing, applying it to both bounds gives the CI at asymptotic level $1 - \alpha$:

. . .

:::{style="font-size: 80%;"}
::: {.square-def}
$$\text{CI}_{1-\alpha}(p_\beta(x)) = \left[\text{logit}^{-1}\left(x^T \hat{\beta} \pm q_{1-\alpha/2} \sqrt{x^T (X^T W_{\hat{\beta}} X)^{-1} x}\right)\right]$$
:::
:::


## Classification

. . .

We have estimated $p_\beta(x) = P(Y = 1|X = x)$ by $p_{\hat{\beta}}(x)$.

. . .

For a [threshold $s \in [0, 1]$ to be chosen]{style="background-color: yellow;"}, we use the rule:

::: {.square-def}
$$\begin{cases}
\text{if } p_{\hat{\beta}}(x) > s, & \hat{Y} = 1 \\
\text{if } p_{\hat{\beta}}(x) \leq s, & \hat{Y} = 0
\end{cases}$$
:::



. . .

The "natural" choice of threshold is $s = 0.5$ but [this choice can be optimized]{style="background-color: yellow;"}.

## Confusion Matrix

. . .

We use a [validation sample]{style="background-color: yellow;"}:

. . .

Fit the model on a [train sample]{style="background-color: yellow;"}, predict $Y$ on a [test sample]{style="background-color: yellow;"}, and form the [confusion matrix]{style="background-color: yellow;"}.

. . .

|        | $Y = 0$ | $Y = 1$ |
|--------|---------|---------|
| $\hat{Y} = 0$ | TN | FN |
| $\hat{Y} = 1$ | FP | TP |

**Reading**: T = true, F = false, N = negative, P = positive.

. . .

**FP** (false positives): number of individuals classified [positive]{style="background-color: yellow;"} who are actually [negative]{style="background-color: orange;"}.


## Sensitivity and Specificity

. . .

Ideally, the confusion matrix is [as diagonal as possible]{style="background-color: yellow;"}.

. . .

We generally seek to maximize the [following indicators]{style="background-color: yellow;"}:

. . .

::: {.columns}
::: {.column}

The **sensitivity** (or recall, or true positive rate) estimates [$\P(\hat{Y} = 1|Y = 1)$]{style="background-color: lightblue;"} by 

::: {.square-def}
$$\frac{\text{TP}}{\text{TP} + \text{FN}}$$
:::

:::
::: {.column}

The **specificity** (or selectivity, or true negative rate) estimates [$\P(\hat{Y} = 0|Y = 0)$]{style="background-color: lightblue;"} by

::: {.square-def}
$$\frac{\text{TN}}{\text{TN} + \text{FP}}$$
:::

:::
::: 


## Other Indicators

. . .

The **precision** (or positive predictive value) estimates $\P(Y = 1|\hat{Y} = 1)$ by 

::: {.square-def}
$\frac{\text{TP}}{\text{TP} + \text{FP}}$
:::
. . .

The **$F$-score** is the harmonic mean of sensitivity and precision:

::: {.square-def}
$$F_1 = 2 \frac{\text{precision} \times \text{sensitivity}}{\text{precision} + \text{sensitivity}}$$
:::

## Choice of Threshold s

. . .

For each threshold $s$, using a test sample, we:

- form the confusion matrix,
- compute scores (sensitivity, $F$-score, etc.).

. . .

Finally, we choose the [optimal threshold $s$]{style="background-color: yellow;"} for the [chosen score]{style="background-color: yellow;"}.


## Choosing the Score

- It depends on the context of the study.
- Wrongly predicting $\hat{Y} = 0$ can be much more serious than wrongly predicting $\hat{Y} = 1$:

. . .


**False positive**: $\hat Y=1$ (treatment) while the patient is [not ill]{style="background-color: yellow;"} ($Y = 0$)

. . .

**False negative**: $\hat Y=0$ (no treatment) while the patient [has a serious illness]{style="background-color: yellow;"} ($Y=1$)

## ROC Curve

. . .

We can also plot the ROC curve (TP rate as a function of FP rate for $s \in [0, 1]$):

:::{style="font-size: 80%;"}
::: {.square-def}
$ROC:~~\mathrm{sensitiv.} = \frac{TP}{TP+FN} = F\left(\frac{FP}{FP+TN}\right) = F(1-\mathrm{specific.})$
:::
:::



. . .

The [AUC (area under the curve)]{style="background-color: yellow;"} is a quality indicator of the model ($0 \leq \text{AUC} \leq 1$).

. . .

Equivalently, one can use the [Gini index: $2 \times \text{AUC} - 1$]{style="background-color: yellow;"}.

. . .

**Use**: compare $2$ models by [plotting the 2 ROC curves]{style="background-color: yellow;"}. 


## ROC Curve Illustration {.smaller}

::: {style="font-size:90%"}
Each threshold $s$ gives one point of the ROC curve. **Drag** the threshold; a better model pulls the curve towards the ideal point.
:::

```{=html}
<div style="text-align:center">
  <canvas id="rocC" width="800" height="330" style="max-width:100%;background:#fff;border:1px solid #ddd;border-radius:8px;touch-action:none"></canvas>
  <div class="lm-row">
    threshold s <input id="rocS" type="range" min="0.01" max="0.99" step="0.01" value="0.5" autocomplete="off" style="vertical-align:middle;width:190px"> <b id="rocSv" style="display:inline-block;width:2.6em">0.50</b>
    &nbsp; model quality <input id="rocD" type="range" min="0" max="5" step="0.05" value="2" autocomplete="off" style="vertical-align:middle;width:150px">
  </div>
  <div class="lm-row" id="rocTxt">–</div>
</div>
<script>
(function () {
  var cv=document.getElementById('rocC'); if(!cv||cv.dataset.init)return; cv.dataset.init=1;
  var c=cv.getContext('2d'),W=cv.width,H=cv.height,KEY='glmRoc';
  var sEl=document.getElementById('rocS'),dEl=document.getElementById('rocD'),sV=document.getElementById('rocSv'),txt=document.getElementById('rocTxt');
  function erf(z){var s=z<0?-1:1;z=Math.abs(z);var t=1/(1+0.3275911*z);return s*(1-((((1.061405429*t-1.453152027)*t+1.421413741)*t-0.284496736)*t+0.254829592)*t*Math.exp(-z*z));}
  function Phi(x){return .5*(1+erf(x/Math.SQRT2));}
  function logit(s){return Math.log(s/(1-s));}
  // scores p̂(x): logit(p̂) ~ N(-δ/2,1) if Y=0, N(+δ/2,1) if Y=1
  function dens(s,mu){var l=logit(s);return Math.exp(-(l-mu)*(l-mu)/2)/2.5066282746/(s*(1-s));}
  var L0=50,L1=470,T=20,B=H-48;           // left panel
  var R0=522,RS=262,RT=20;                // ROC square
  function SX(s){return L0+s*(L1-L0);} function ISX(px){return (px-L0)/(L1-L0);}
  function FX(f){return R0+f*RS;} function FY(t){return RT+RS-t*RS;}
  function pos(e){var r=cv.getBoundingClientRect();return [(e.clientX-r.left)*W/r.width,(e.clientY-r.top)*H/r.height];}
  function rates(s,d){var l=logit(s);return {tpr:1-Phi(l-d/2),fpr:1-Phi(l+d/2)};}
  function draw(){
    var s=+sEl.value,d=+dEl.value;sV.textContent=s.toFixed(2);
    c.clearRect(0,0,W,H);c.fillStyle='#fff';c.fillRect(0,0,W,H);c.lineWidth=1;
    // ---- score densities
    var M=400,mx=0,g0=[],g1=[];
    for(var i=1;i<M;i++){var u=i/M,a=dens(u,-d/2),b=dens(u,d/2);g0.push([u,a]);g1.push([u,b]);mx=Math.max(mx,a,b);}
    mx=Math.min(mx,12)*1.08;
    function DY(v){return B-Math.min(v,mx)/mx*(B-T);}
    function area(g,from,to,col){c.beginPath();c.moveTo(SX(from),B);g.forEach(function(q){if(q[0]>=from&&q[0]<=to)c.lineTo(SX(q[0]),DY(q[1]));});c.lineTo(SX(to),B);c.closePath();c.fillStyle=col;c.fill();}
    function curve(g,col){c.beginPath();g.forEach(function(q,j){j?c.lineTo(SX(q[0]),DY(q[1])):c.moveTo(SX(q[0]),DY(q[1]));});c.strokeStyle=col;c.lineWidth=2;c.stroke();c.lineWidth=1;}
    c.save();c.beginPath();c.rect(L0,T,L1-L0,B-T);c.clip();
    area(g0,0,s,'rgba(52,152,219,.10)');area(g0,s,1,'rgba(52,152,219,.38)');
    area(g1,0,s,'rgba(231,76,60,.10)');area(g1,s,1,'rgba(231,76,60,.38)');
    curve(g0,'#3498db');curve(g1,'#e74c3c');
    c.restore();
    c.strokeStyle='#ccc';c.beginPath();c.moveTo(L0,B);c.lineTo(L1,B);c.stroke();
    c.font='13px sans-serif';c.fillStyle='#666';c.textAlign='center';c.textBaseline='top';
    for(var t=0;t<=1.001;t+=.25)c.fillText(t.toFixed(2).replace(/0$/,'').replace(/\.0$/,''),SX(t),B+5);
    c.fillStyle='#333';c.font='14px sans-serif';c.fillText('score = predicted probability',(L0+L1)/2,B+24);
    // threshold
    c.strokeStyle='#2c3e50';c.lineWidth=2.5;c.beginPath();c.moveTo(SX(s),T);c.lineTo(SX(s),B);c.stroke();c.lineWidth=1;
    c.fillStyle='#2c3e50';c.beginPath();c.arc(SX(s),T+6,6,0,7);c.fill();
    c.textBaseline='middle';c.font='13px sans-serif';
    c.textAlign='right';c.fillStyle='#555';c.fillText('Ŷ = 0  ←',SX(s)-8,T+6);
    c.textAlign='left';c.fillText('→  Ŷ = 1',SX(s)+8,T+6);
    c.font='bold 13px sans-serif';
    c.fillStyle='#2471a3';c.textAlign='left';c.fillText('Y = 0',L0+8,T+34);
    c.fillStyle='#c0392b';c.textAlign='right';c.fillText('Y = 1',L1-8,T+34);
    // ---- ROC
    var r=rates(s,d);
    c.strokeStyle='#ccc';c.strokeRect(FX(0),FY(1),RS,RS);
    c.setLineDash([4,4]);c.beginPath();c.moveTo(FX(0),FY(0));c.lineTo(FX(1),FY(1));c.stroke();c.setLineDash([]);
    var roc=[];for(i=-400;i<=400;i++){roc.push(rates(1/(1+Math.exp(-i/40)),d));}
    roc.sort(function(p,q){return p.fpr-q.fpr;});
    c.beginPath();c.moveTo(FX(0),FY(0));roc.forEach(function(q){c.lineTo(FX(q.fpr),FY(q.tpr));});c.lineTo(FX(1),FY(1));c.lineTo(FX(1),FY(0));c.closePath();c.fillStyle='rgba(52,152,219,.10)';c.fill();
    c.beginPath();c.moveTo(FX(0),FY(0));roc.forEach(function(q){c.lineTo(FX(q.fpr),FY(q.tpr));});c.lineTo(FX(1),FY(1));c.strokeStyle='#2c3e50';c.lineWidth=2.2;c.stroke();c.lineWidth=1;
    c.strokeStyle='rgba(231,76,60,.6)';c.setLineDash([3,3]);c.beginPath();c.moveTo(FX(r.fpr),FY(0));c.lineTo(FX(r.fpr),FY(r.tpr));c.lineTo(FX(0),FY(r.tpr));c.stroke();c.setLineDash([]);
    c.beginPath();c.arc(FX(r.fpr),FY(r.tpr),6,0,7);c.fillStyle='#e74c3c';c.fill();
    c.fillStyle='#e74c3c';c.font='13px sans-serif';c.textAlign='left';c.textBaseline='middle';
    c.beginPath();c.arc(FX(0),FY(1),4,0,7);c.fill();c.fillText('ideal point',FX(0)+8,FY(1)+12);
    c.fillStyle='#777';c.fillText('s = 1',FX(0)+8,FY(0)-10);c.textAlign='right';c.fillText('s = 0',FX(1)-6,FY(1)+12);
    c.fillStyle='#666';c.textAlign='center';c.textBaseline='top';c.font='12px sans-serif';
    c.fillText('0',FX(0),FY(0)+4);c.fillText('1',FX(1),FY(0)+4);
    c.fillStyle='#333';c.font='13px sans-serif';c.fillText('FP rate = 1 − specificity',FX(.5),FY(0)+20);
    c.save();c.translate(FX(0)-18,FY(.5));c.rotate(-Math.PI/2);c.textBaseline='middle';c.fillText('TP rate = sensitivity',0,0);c.restore();
    var auc=Phi(d/Math.SQRT2);
    txt.innerHTML='sensitivity <b>'+r.tpr.toFixed(2)+'</b> &nbsp;·&nbsp; specificity <b>'+(1-r.fpr).toFixed(2)+'</b> &nbsp;·&nbsp; AUC <b>'+auc.toFixed(3)+'</b> &nbsp;·&nbsp; Gini <b>'+(2*auc-1).toFixed(3)+'</b> &nbsp; <span style="opacity:.7">(dark blue: FP, dark red: TP)</span>';
    try{localStorage.setItem(KEY,JSON.stringify({s:s,d:d}));}catch(e){}
  }
  var drag=false;
  cv.addEventListener('pointerdown',function(e){var p=pos(e);if(p[0]>=L0-10&&p[0]<=L1+10&&p[1]<=B){drag=true;cv.setPointerCapture(e.pointerId);sEl.value=Math.max(.01,Math.min(.99,ISX(p[0])));draw();}});
  cv.addEventListener('pointermove',function(e){if(!drag)return;var p=pos(e);sEl.value=Math.max(.01,Math.min(.99,ISX(p[0])));draw();e.preventDefault();});
  window.addEventListener('pointerup',function(){drag=false;});
  sEl.addEventListener('input',draw);dEl.addEventListener('input',draw);
  try{var sv=JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem(KEY));if(sv){sEl.value=sv.s;dEl.value=sv.d;}}catch(e){}
  draw();
})();
</script>
```

## Summary of the Chapter

- **Model**: $Y|X=x \sim \mathcal B(p(x))$ with $\text{logit}\, p(x) = x^T\beta$
- **Interpretation**: $e^{\beta_j}$ is the odds ratio for a one-unit increase of $x^{(j)}$, other regressors fixed
- **Estimation**: MLE computed numerically; unique if $\text{rank}(X) = p$, exists if and only if the classes overlap
- **Inference**: Wald tests and CIs (asymptotic normality), deviance tests for nested models, AIC/BIC
- **Prediction**: CI for $p(x)$, classification with a threshold $s$, ROC curve and AUC
